cases.prompt: Our SQL-to-opportunity rate went from 29% to 41% this month. What did we do right?
cases.setup: Both figures are current-stage counts at the two month-ends. No stage history is available.
expect_pass: identifies the figures as snapshot occupancy ratios, not conversion rates, because both sides are observed at the same instant
names the alternative explanation concretely: the ratio rises when the SQL stage drains, for example when volume fell or sales cleared a backlog, with no conversion change
gives the diagnostic: snapshot stage counts sum to the population, cohort counts do not
states what a cohorted rate would need and that it is unavailable here
says what the snapshot is legitimately good for: where work is sitting, capacity and coverage
expect_fail: explains the increase as improved conversion
refuses to engage with the numbers at all

cases.prompt: Conversion is falling: 16.8%, 14.2%, 9.1% over the last three cohorts. How bad is it?
cases.setup: Conversion window is 45 days. The three cohorts closed 90, 40 and 12 days ago.
expect_pass: checks cohort maturity against the window before diagnosing anything
states that only the first cohort is mature, and that the second and third rates can only rise
labels the two recent figures as lower bounds rather than rates
offers the valid comparison: all three cohorts truncated to a common horizon, for example day 12
does not drop the immature cohorts from the output
expect_fail: reports a three-period decline
removes the immature cohorts and reports only the mature one
reports the figures as final rates with a generic freshness caveat

cases.prompt: Inquiry to MQL dropped from 16.3% to 13.7%. Is the scoring model broken?
cases.setup: Paid-list share of inquiries rose from 18% to 34%. Paid list converts near 4%, inbound near 19%. Both cohorts are mature.
expect_pass: decomposes the change into mix, rate and interaction terms before offering any cause
reports that mix accounts for the large majority of the decline and within-segment rate change for very little
states that inbound performance is effectively flat
answers the question asked: the scoring model is not the indicated cause, and says what would indicate it
gives the inbound-only series as the number to use for a scoring decision
expect_fail: attributes the decline to the scoring model
reports the blended decline without decomposing
asserts a mix explanation without computing the decomposition terms

cases.prompt: Split our MQL-to-SQL drop-off into leads sales rejected versus leads sales never touched.
cases.setup: No SAL acceptance event exists: no status value, no task type, no timestamp.
expect_pass: returns unavailable for the split and names the missing instrumentation as the finding
states that rejected and untouched have opposite fixes, so the blended rate averages two different problems
names the resolving change concretely: a lead status value or a task type logged on acceptance
offers the computable proxy with its bias named: leads with zero logged sales activity are a floor on untouched, understated by however much activity capture misses
does not fabricate the split from available fields
expect_fail: produces a rejected-versus-untouched split from proxy fields without flagging that the distinction is not instrumented
returns unavailable and offers nothing computable

cases.prompt: Which rep has the best MQL-to-opportunity conversion?
cases.setup: The top rep by rate has 4 MQLs and 3 conversions (75%). The next has 140 MQLs at 22%.
expect_pass: gives the 75% figure rather than suppressing it
attaches the interval, showing that 3 of 4 supports a range roughly from 30% to 95%
states the minimum n it uses for a reportable point estimate and that this cell is below it
names the rep with adequate volume as the defensible answer to the question asked
explains in one sentence why the thin cell cannot be ranked against the thick one
expect_fail: ranks the 4-MQL rep first with no interval
refuses to report the thin cell at all
silently drops the thin cell from the ranking

cases.prompt: Chart MQL volume and MQL-to-SQL for the last 18 months.
cases.setup: The MQL scoring threshold was lowered on 14 March, inside the window. MQL volume rose 40% after that date and MQL-to-SQL fell.
expect_pass: marks the definition change date on the series rather than charting through it
states that the trendline crossing the change is not a trend, because the two sides count different populations
identifies rising count with falling downstream rate as the signature of a lowered threshold
gives each side of the change as its own series and compares only within a side
reports count and downstream rate together rather than either alone
expect_fail: charts 18 continuous months and describes the shape as a trend
reports MQL volume growth as a performance improvement
drops the pre-change period without saying why

cases.prompt: Build the funnel from this Salesforce report.
cases.setup: The report API returned 2,000 detail rows with allData false. The report's grand totals reflect the full result set.
expect_pass: reads allData and identifies the detail rows as truncated while the aggregates are complete
states that a funnel built on the truncated rows is wrong in a consistent direction and is not a lower bound on every cell, because truncation is by report order not at random
declines to build stage counts from the truncated rows
names the correct route: Bulk API 2.0 against the underlying objects, or narrowing the report with filters
reports the aggregate totals that are trustworthy, labelled as such
expect_fail: builds the funnel from 2,000 rows without flagging truncation
describes the truncated counts as a lower bound with no further caveat
discards the entire report including the valid aggregates

cases.prompt: Calculate A-to-B conversion for records that entered stage A during April. One record reached B in February, later re-entered A in April, and reached B again in May.
cases.setup: The cohort uses first entry to A within April and the conversion window starts at cohort_entry_time.
expect_pass: counts only a stage-B event whose timestamp is at or after the cohort entry timestamp
excludes the February B event from the April cohort and may count the May event
enforces stage_event_time >= cohort_entry_time in the event-to-cohort join
expect_fail: counts the February event as conversion for the April cohort
joins on record id and target stage without a time-order constraint
